answer.rationale:
The loudest signal (competitor entry pricing) points at promotional_pricing via memory_73, but that memory is the weakest-provenance item in the inherited set: a four-week readout on the standard SMB segment with 'the usual reporting cadence.' Four weeks is long enough to capture acquisition and booked revenue but too short to see discount-driven churn, margin erosion, or whether the acquired accounts were price-shoppers who never reach durable value. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is exactly the kind of claim that can be true on the metric it was measured on and still wrong for the decision. So it is my first verification pull rather than my default action.

My intended action instead targets the two things actually degrading: onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%). memory_86 and memory_31 both support reducing friction in the early path, and memory_91 is a plausible adjacent lever. But memory_86 and memory_31 may share a single failure mode rather than being independent confirmation: shortening onboarding and cutting signup fields can raise completion and week-one activation partly by removing the steps that qualified and enriched the account. If so, the lift is real at the top and hollow downstream, and stacking another reduction would compound the damage precisely where I am supposed to be maximizing qualified revenue. Hence memory_86 as the second pull, specifically to see whether the original record tracked anything past week one and whether lead quality or paid conversion was instrumented at all.

I am committing to simplify_onboarding at standard experiment scale, not broad rollout, and with downstream guardrails (paid conversion, 60-90 day retention, lead-quality proxies) as gating metrics rather than post-hoc reporting. If memory_86 turns out to have measured only completion and week-one adoption, I will narrow to a small guarded test and treat the inherited claim as unreplicated rather than as established fact. Enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is plausible but addresses neither current decline; referral_incentive (memory_57) is scoped to established customers and does not touch the SMB pressure or the activation drop.

Uncertainty I am explicitly not collapsing: I do not yet know whether the activation and onboarding declines are the same underlying cause (a shared funnel regression) or two independent effects, and I do not know whether the competitor is drawing off accounts that would have become qualified revenue or accounts that were never going to convert. Either answer would change the ranking, and one experiment slot will not resolve both.
